Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: CNS Tumor Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Brain tumors come in two broad flavors: tumors that start in the CNS (primary tumors: gliomas, meningiomas, schwannomas, pituitary tumors, lymphoma) and tumors that spread there from cancer elsewhere (brain metastases, by far the most common). Radiation treats almost all of them, benign and malignant. Before anatomy or treatment, get straight how common each is, who gets them, and how they present.

How Common Are Brain Tumors?

Metastases >50%

Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumor in adults. 20–40% of cancer patients develop them; most have multiple lesions.

Meningioma ~40%

The most common primary brain tumor. Usually benign (WHO grade 1), more common in women.

Glioblastoma

The most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Median age ~65, median survival only ~15 months with treatment.

TumorTypical patientBehavior
Brain metastasesAdults with lung (most common), breast, melanoma (highest propensity), kidney, colorectal cancerDepends on the primary and systemic disease
MeningiomaMiddle-aged/older women; prior cranial RT~80% grade 1 (benign); grade 2–3 recur
Glioblastoma (grade 4)~65 years, slight male predominanceAggressive; almost always recurs
IDH-mutant gliomas (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma)Younger adults (30s–40s), seizuresSlower; survival often many years
Vestibular schwannomaMiddle-aged adults; bilateral = NF2Benign, slow-growing
Pituitary adenomaAdults; often incidentalBenign; can secrete hormones
Primary CNS lymphomaOlder adults; immunosuppressed (HIV, transplant: EBV)Very responsive to chemo and RT
PediatricBrain tumors are the most common solid tumor of childhoodPilocytic astrocytoma (most common glioma), medulloblastoma (most common malignant), ependymoma, DIPG
Clinical Pearl

Don't mix up "most common primary CNS tumor" (meningioma), "most common malignant primary" (glioblastoma), and "most common brain tumor overall" (metastases).

Risk Factors

1
Ionizing Radiation

The only established environmental cause. Childhood cranial RT raises the risk of meningioma (most), glioma, and sarcoma, often decades later. Cell phones: no proven link.

2
Immunosuppression

HIV and transplant: EBV-driven primary CNS lymphoma.

3
Hormones

Meningiomas are more common in women, can grow in pregnancy, and express progesterone receptors.

4
Genetic Syndromes

Rare but high-yield (table below).

SyndromeGeneCNS tumors
NF1NF1 (17q)Optic pathway glioma, astrocytomas, neurofibromas, MPNST
NF2NF2/merlin (22q)Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, spinal ependymomas
Li-FraumeniTP53Gliomas, choroid plexus carcinoma, medulloblastoma
Von Hippel-LindauVHL (3p)Hemangioblastoma (cerebellum, retina)
Tuberous sclerosisTSC1/TSC2Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
GorlinPTCH1Medulloblastoma (avoid RT when possible: basal cell cancers)
Turcot / Lynch, FAPMMR / APCGlioblastoma (Lynch) / medulloblastoma (FAP)

Classification Instead of Stage

Most brain tumors don't spread outside the CNS, so there's no TNM staging. Instead they're described by WHO type and grade (1–4), which since WHO 2021 depends heavily on molecular markers. For gliomas, one test sorts everything:

1
IDH wild-type → glioblastoma (grade 4)
→
2
IDH mutant + 1p/19q codeleted → oligodendroglioma (2–3)
→
3
IDH mutant, 1p/19q intact → astrocytoma (2–4)

The full classification, the grading features, and the molecular upgrades are in Workup & Staging.

How Brain Tumors Present

SymptomWhat it suggests
Headache worse in the morning or when lying down, with nausea/vomitingRaised intracranial pressure (mass effect, edema, hydrocephalus)
SeizureCortical tumor, especially low-grade glioma and oligodendroglioma
Focal deficit (weakness, aphasia, visual field cut)Localizes the lesion (see Neuroanatomy)
Personality or cognitive changeFrontal lobe or corpus callosum
Hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalanceVestibular schwannoma
Bitemporal hemianopia, hormone problemsPituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma
Back pain + leg weakness, bladder/bowel changeSpinal cord compression: an emergency
Self-check: a patient with metastatic melanoma has a sudden severe headache and a new brain lesion that is bright on CT. What happened?▾

A hemorrhagic metastasis. Melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid cancer mets tend to bleed.

High-Yield Summary
  • Brain metastases are the most common brain tumor, meningioma is the most common primary tumor, and glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary.
  • IDH-mutant gliomas occur in younger patients, often present with seizures, and have much longer survival than IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.
  • The only established environmental risk factor is ionizing radiation, and immunosuppression raises the risk of primary CNS lymphoma.
  • NF1 causes optic gliomas, NF2 causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas, and VHL causes hemangioblastomas.
  • Brain tumors have no TNM staging; they are classified by WHO type and grade, driven by IDH and 1p/19q status.

Neuroanatomy.title: Neuroanatomy: Brain Levels, Skull Base & Spine
Neuroanatomy.html:
Brain radiation is anatomy-heavy. You need to localize a lesion from the symptoms, name the structures on every scan, and know which nearby structures are organs at risk. There are no lymph nodes to learn here. Instead, this page builds the brain from the outside in: the lobes and what they do, the midline and the brainstem, the deep structures and coverings, then the organs at risk and the spine. Every structure here shows up again on MRI in the Imaging section.

The Big Picture: Lobes, Midline, and Underside

The Lobes and What They Do

  • Each hemisphere has four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal; the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe below.
  • The precentral gyrus (just in front of the central sulcus) is the motor strip; the postcentral gyrus (just behind it) is the sensory strip. Both are mapped like the homunculus: the leg near the midline, the face and hand out to the side.
  • Each hemisphere runs the opposite side of the body. The cerebellum is the exception: it controls the same side.
  • Language lives in the dominant hemisphere (the left in almost all right-handed people): Broca's area (frontal) to speak, Wernicke's area (temporal) to understand.

Localizing a Lesion

LocationFunctionA lesion causes
FrontalExecutive function, personality, motor strip, Broca's (dominant)Personality change, contralateral weakness, expressive aphasia, seizures
ParietalSensory strip, spatial awarenessContralateral numbness, neglect (non-dominant), inferior quadrantanopia
TemporalHearing, Wernicke's (dominant), memory (hippocampus)Receptive aphasia, memory loss, seizures with aura, superior quadrantanopia
OccipitalVisionContralateral homonymous hemianopia
CerebellumCoordinationIpsilateral ataxia, dysmetria; hydrocephalus (4th ventricle)
BrainstemCranial nerves, long tracts, consciousnessCrossed signs: cranial nerve palsy + contralateral body weakness

The Midline and the Brainstem

  • The corpus callosum is the bridge between the hemispheres. A tumor that crosses it to the other side is usually a glioblastoma or lymphoma.
  • The diencephalon sits in the middle: the thalamus (the sensory relay station) and, below it, the hypothalamus, which controls the pituitary hanging beneath it.
  • The brainstem has three parts, and each holds the nuclei for a set of cranial nerves:
Part Cranial nerves What else it does
MidbrainIII, IVEye movements; holds the cerebral aqueduct
PonsV, VI, VII, VIIIRelays signals to the cerebellum; sits in front of the 4th ventricle
MedullaIX, X, XI, XIIBreathing, heart rate, swallowing
Brainstem cranial nerves come in a 2-4-4 pattern: midbrain has 2 (III, IV), pons has 4 (V to VIII), medulla has 4 (IX to XII).

Blood Supply

Artery Territory A stroke here causes
Anterior cerebral (ACA)Medial frontal and parietal lobesLeg weakness on the opposite side
Middle cerebral (MCA)Most of the lateral hemisphereFace and arm weakness, aphasia (dominant side)
Posterior cerebral (PCA)Occipital lobe, inferior temporal lobe, thalamusHomonymous hemianopia

Knowing the territories helps you tell a stroke (wedge-shaped, follows one artery) from a tumor (doesn't respect territories) on imaging.

Deep Structures, Ventricles, and Compartments

Gray Matter, White Matter, and the Deep Nuclei

  • Gray matter is the cell bodies: the cortex on the surface and the deep nuclei (thalamus and basal ganglia) inside. White matter is the wiring between them.
  • The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus) control movement. The internal capsule is the narrow white matter lane between them and the thalamus that carries the motor fibers, so a small lesion there causes a large weakness.
  • The hippocampus sits on the inner surface of the temporal lobe, next to the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. It forms new memories, which is why hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain RT spares it.
  • Tumors in deep structures (thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) usually can't be removed safely and are biopsied instead.

The Coverings and the Tentorium

  • Three layers of meninges cover the brain and cord: the tough dura, the thin arachnoid, and the pia on the brain surface. CSF flows in the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia.
  • The dura folds inward in two places: the falx cerebri between the hemispheres, and the tentorium cerebelli between the cerebrum and cerebellum.
  • The tentorium splits the skull into the supratentorial space (the cerebrum) and the infratentorial posterior fossa (the cerebellum and brainstem). Most adult brain tumors are supratentorial; most childhood brain tumors are in the posterior fossa.
  • Tumors are also described as intra-axial (inside the brain tissue, like gliomas and metastases) or extra-axial (outside it, from the coverings or nerves, like meningiomas and schwannomas). That one distinction narrows the differential a lot.

CSF Flow and Hydrocephalus

1
Lateral ventricles
→
2
Foramina of Monro → 3rd ventricle
→
3
Cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle
→
4
Luschka / Magendie → subarachnoid space
  • A mass that blocks the flow (posterior fossa tumor, pineal tumor, colloid cyst) causes obstructive hydrocephalus: headache, vomiting, papilledema. It needs a shunt or ventriculostomy before RT.
  • Tumors that spread through CSF (medulloblastoma, some germ cell tumors, ependymoma, leptomeningeal disease) need the whole CSF space treated: craniospinal irradiation down to the thecal sac (~S2).

Organs at Risk

Organ Where it sits Toxicity
Optic nerves / chiasmOrbit to the suprasellar cistern, above the pituitaryBlindness
BrainstemMidbrain, pons, and medulla, in front of the 4th ventricleNecrosis, cranial neuropathy
Spinal cordForamen magnum down to L1–L2Myelopathy
CochleaInner ear, lateral to the internal auditory canalHearing loss
HippocampusMedial temporal lobeMemory loss
LensFront of the eyeCataract
Retina / lacrimal glandBack of the eye / upper outer orbitRetinopathy / dry eye
Pituitary / hypothalamusSella and the floor of the 3rd ventricleHormone deficits
Normal brainEverywhere around the targetRadionecrosis, cognitive decline
The 54 Gy club: chiasm, optic nerves, and brainstem all top out near 54 Gy with conventional fractionation.

The Spine

  • The cord ends at L1–L2 (conus medullaris); below that is the cauda equina. The thecal sac ends at ~S2 (bottom of a craniospinal field).
  • Most spine metastases start in the vertebral body and grow back into the epidural space, compressing the cord (graded by Bilsky 0–3).
  • The cord is shorter than the spine, so cord segments sit higher than the vertebrae with the same number, especially in the lower back.
  • The spinal cord is an organ at risk in any field that crosses it: head and neck, lung, esophagus, and every spine metastasis.
High-Yield Summary
  • The frontal lobe controls personality and movement, the parietal lobe sensation, the temporal lobe hearing, language, and memory, the occipital lobe vision, and the cerebellum coordination on the same side.
  • The brainstem runs from the midbrain (CN III and IV) to the pons (CN V to VIII) to the medulla (CN IX to XII), and it is one of the most important organs at risk.
  • The tentorium divides the skull into the supratentorial space, where most adult tumors arise, and the infratentorial posterior fossa, where most childhood tumors arise.
  • CSF flows from the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle and through the aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, so posterior fossa masses cause hydrocephalus.
  • The spinal cord ends at L1 to L2 and the thecal sac ends at S2, which sets the bottom of a craniospinal field.

Imaging.title: CNS Imaging: MRI, CT & Advanced Imaging
Imaging.html:
MRI with contrast is the workhorse for almost every CNS tumor: it makes the diagnosis look likely, guides surgery, and is the scan we plan on (fused with the planning CT). CT is the fast first scan in the ER and shows bone, calcium, and blood. Advanced MRI and PET help after treatment. This section comes before Workup & Classification because most CNS diagnoses start with a picture.

ModalityThe question it answersWhen you'll see it
MRI brain with/without contrastWhat is it, where, how big, how many?Every brain tumor; thin-slice for SRS
CT headBleeding? Hydrocephalus? Calcium or bone?ER first look; RT simulation
MRI spineCord compression? Drop metastases?Back pain + neuro symptoms; craniospinal staging
Perfusion, spectroscopy, amino-acid PETTumor or treatment effect?Growing enhancement after RT
FDG PET/CT bodyWhere's the primary? Other disease?Brain mets of unknown origin; lymphoma staging

MRI Sequences: What Each One Shows

SequenceBright = Main use
T1 post-contrastEnhancing tissue (broken blood-brain barrier)High-grade tumor, mets, meningioma, schwannoma: the GTV
T2 / FLAIRWater: edema and infiltrative tumor (FLAIR suppresses CSF)Low-grade glioma extent; edema; the CTV region for gliomas
DWI / ADCRestricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC)Dense tumors (lymphoma, medulloblastoma), abscess, stroke
SWI / GREDark = blood or calciumHemorrhagic mets, calcified oligodendroglioma
Perfusion (rCBV)Blood volumeHigh in tumor, low in radionecrosis

Normal Anatomy on MRI: Level by Level

LevelLandmarksWhy it matters for RT
1. Centrum semiovaleWhite matter sheet, motor "hand knob," falx, superior sagittal sinusLeukoencephalopathy after WBRT; parasagittal meningiomas
2. Lateral ventricle bodiesCorpus callosum, caudate, corona radiataCallosal crossing = GBM or lymphoma; periventricular lymphoma
3. Basal ganglia / thalamusInternal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, insula, 3rd ventricleDeep, unresectable tumors (biopsy only)
4. Midbrain / suprasellarCerebral peduncles, aqueduct, optic chiasm, hippocampi, temporal lobesChiasm and hippocampal sparing
5. Pons / CPAPons, internal auditory canals, cochlea, 4th ventricle, cerebellumVestibular schwannoma, brainstem and cochlea limits
6. Medulla / foramen magnumMedulla, tonsils, clivus, jugular foramenChordoma, glomus tumors, tonsillar herniation
Self-check: on an axial MRI at the level of the internal auditory canals, which three organs at risk would you contour?▾

The brainstem (pons), both cochleae, and the temporal lobes (plus the cerebellum and facial nerve region depending on the target).

Sella, Orbits, and Spine on MRI

  • The pituitary is best seen on thin coronal slices: look for the chiasm above it and the cavernous sinuses on either side.
  • On orbit images, the lens is dark and the vitreous bright on T2; the optic nerves run back to the chiasm.
  • On a sagittal spine MRI, follow the cord down to the conus at L1–L2 and the thecal sac to S2.

Gliomas

High grade
Glioblastoma
  • Thick, irregular ring enhancement around necrosis
  • Lots of FLAIR edema/infiltration
  • Can cross the corpus callosum ("butterfly")
  • Mass effect, midline shift
Low grade
IDH-mutant glioma
  • Non-enhancing, FLAIR-bright, expansile
  • Little edema or mass effect
  • T2-FLAIR mismatch = IDH-mutant astrocytoma
  • Calcification (CT) = oligodendroglioma
  • Get the MRI within 48–72 hours after surgery to judge the extent of resection before postoperative changes set in.
  • For GBM planning: GTV = enhancing tumor + resection cavity (± FLAIR); CTV = GTV + ~1.5–2 cm, trimmed at anatomic barriers (bone, falx, tentorium).

Brain Metastases and SRS Planning

  • Mets are round, sit at the gray-white junction, and have edema out of proportion to their size. Often multiple.
  • A thin-slice (1–1.5 mm) contrast MRI within ~1–2 weeks of SRS finds more lesions than routine MRI.
  • Hemorrhagic mets: melanoma, renal, choriocarcinoma, thyroid.
  • SRS dose limits: V12 of normal brain (radionecrosis), optic apparatus ≤8–10 Gy, brainstem ~12–15 Gy.
Self-check: a ring-enhancing lesion with bright DWI (restricted diffusion) in the center. Tumor or abscess?▾

Central restricted diffusion favors an abscess (pus). A necrotic tumor usually has facilitated (dark) diffusion in the center. Lymphoma restricts diffusion but enhances solidly.

Benign Tumors: Meningioma, Schwannoma, Pituitary

TumorSignature findingsWhat limits RT
MeningiomaExtra-axial, homogeneous enhancement, dural tail, CSF cleft, hyperostosis, calcificationLocation (optic apparatus near skull base tumors)
Vestibular schwannoma"Ice cream cone": widens the IAC and fills the CPA; cystic change when largeCochlea (hearing), brainstem, CN VII
Pituitary macroadenoma"Snowman" sellar/suprasellar mass; compresses the chiasm; cavernous sinus invasionOptic chiasm (just above)
CraniopharyngiomaSuprasellar, cystic + solid + calcified ("motor oil" cyst fluid)Chiasm, hypothalamus; cysts can grow during RT

CT, Treatment Effect, and the Spine

After Radiation: Tumor or Treatment Effect?

Pseudoprogression
Early (within ~3 months)

More enhancement right after chemoRT for GBM, especially MGMT-methylated tumors. Settles on its own. Don't stop treatment for one scan: repeat the MRI.

Radionecrosis
Late (6 months to years)

After SRS or high dose. "Soap bubble" enhancement, low rCBV. Treated with steroids, bevacizumab, or laser ablation.

True progression shows high rCBV on perfusion, a high choline/NAA ratio on spectroscopy, and uptake on amino-acid PET. The RANO criteria formalize response for gliomas.

The Spine

  • Back pain + leg weakness or bladder/bowel change in a cancer patient = MRI of the whole spine now (multiple levels are common).
  • Bilsky grade: 0–1 = bone or epidural disease without cord deformity; 2–3 = high-grade compression. SINS scores spinal stability.
High-Yield Summary
  • MRI with contrast is the main test for almost every brain tumor, and CT is used for bleeding, hydrocephalus, bone, and simulation.
  • Enhancement on T1 post-contrast is the tumor (GTV), and T2/FLAIR signal shows edema and infiltrating tumor.
  • Glioblastoma shows thick ring enhancement with central necrosis, while metastases are round, sit at the gray-white junction, and have a lot of edema.
  • Meningiomas have a dural tail, vestibular schwannomas look like an ice cream cone, and pituitary macroadenomas look like a snowman pushing up on the chiasm.
  • After treatment, pseudoprogression (early) and radiation necrosis (late) can both look like tumor growth, and perfusion imaging helps tell them apart.

Workup & Classification.title: CNS Workup, Classification & Grading
Workup & Classification.html:
CNS "staging" is simpler than other sites: there's no TNM. For any brain or spine lesion, three questions decide the plan:

1
What is it?

Histology, WHO grade, and molecular markers, or a confident imaging diagnosis for benign tumors (meningioma, schwannoma).

2
Where and how big?

Eloquent brain? Near the chiasm, brainstem, cochlea? How many lesions? Hydrocephalus or cord compression?

3
How is the patient?

KPS, age, neurologic deficits, and (for mets) systemic disease control. These drive prognosis scores like the GPA.

The bottom of this page has the NCCN workup and grading tables.

The Core Workup

  1. History and neuro exam: symptoms, seizures, focal deficits, KPS.
  2. MRI brain with and without contrast (CT first if unstable or MRI isn't possible).
  3. Dexamethasone for symptomatic edema, but hold steroids if lymphoma is suspected until after biopsy. Antiseizure medicine only if the patient has had a seizure.
  4. Tissue: maximal safe resection (diagnosis + treatment) or stereotactic biopsy for deep/eloquent tumors. Benign-looking meningiomas and schwannomas are often treated on imaging alone.
  5. Molecular testing for gliomas: IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, ATRX, TP53, TERT, EGFR, CDKN2A/B, H3 K27M.
  6. Site-specific extras: body CT or PET for mets; audiogram for vestibular schwannoma; visual fields and pituitary hormones for sellar tumors; spine MRI + CSF cytology for tumors that spread through CSF; HIV test and eye exam for lymphoma.

Gliomas: WHO 2021 Classification and Grading

TumorMolecular definitionWHO grade
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtypeIDH wild-type + (necrosis or microvascular proliferation, or TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/−10)4
Astrocytoma, IDH-mutantIDH mutant, 1p/19q intact (usually ATRX loss, TP53 mutation)2, 3, or 4 (4 if necrosis/MVP or CDKN2A/B deletion)
OligodendrogliomaIDH mutant + 1p/19q codeleted2 or 3
Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-alteredH3 K27M (pons/thalamus/spine; children and young adults)4
  • Histologic grading ("MEAN"): Mitoses, Endothelial (microvascular) proliferation, nuclear Atypia, Necrosis. Atypia = grade 2; + mitoses = grade 3; necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation = grade 4.
  • Molecular trumps the microscope: an IDH-wildtype tumor that looks grade 2 is still GBM if it has a TERT mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/−10.
  • MGMT promoter methylation is prognostic and predicts benefit from temozolomide.
  • IDH mutation is the strongest good prognostic factor; oligodendrogliomas do best.
Quick check: IDH-mutant, 1p/19q intact, histologically grade 3, but CDKN2A/B homozygously deleted. Diagnosis?▾

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4. CDKN2A/B deletion upgrades it. It's not called glioblastoma, because GBM is IDH-wildtype by definition.

Brain Metastases: Count, Size, and Prognosis

  • Workup: thin-slice MRI (count every lesion), body staging (CT or PET), and tissue if there's no known cancer or it's been years since the primary.
  • What drives the plan: number and size of lesions, total volume, symptoms/mass effect, KPS, systemic disease and options (e.g., targeted therapy with CNS activity for EGFR/ALK lung cancer).
  • Prognosis is estimated with the GPA (Graded Prognostic Assessment). The newer diagnosis-specific GPA adds the cancer type and markers.

A Tour of Everything Else Radiation Treats

Brain radiation isn't just gliomas and mets. You'll see all of these on service:

EntityHow it's graded or describedWhere RT fits
MeningiomaWHO 1 (~80%), 2 (atypical): brain invasion or 4–19 mitoses/10 HPF, 3 (anaplastic): ≥20 mitoses, TERT, CDKN2A/B. Extent of resection = Simpson grade I–VObserve small/asymptomatic; RT (SRS or fractionated) for residual, recurrent, unresectable, or grade 2–3
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)Size and Koos grade I–IV (IV compresses the brainstem); hearing classObserve (serial MRI); SRS 12–13 Gy for growing small/medium tumors; surgery for large
Pituitary adenomaMicro (<1 cm) vs macro (≥1 cm); functioning (prolactin, GH, ACTH) vs nonfunctioningSurgery (or cabergoline for prolactinoma); RT for residual/recurrent
CraniopharyngiomaAdamantinomatous (children, calcified, CTNNB1) vs papillary (adults, BRAF V600E)Limited surgery + RT (50.4–54 Gy)
Primary CNS lymphomaDiffuse large B-cell; stage the eye, CSF, and bodyHigh-dose methotrexate first; WBRT for consolidation/salvage
MedulloblastomaChang M stage (M0 none → M1 CSF → M2 brain → M3 spine → M4 outside CNS); standard vs high riskCraniospinal RT + boost + chemo
EpendymomaLocation + molecular group (e.g., PFA, ZFTA)Resection + focal RT (~54–59.4 Gy)
Spine metastases / cord compressionBilsky (epidural compression), SINS (stability), NOMS frameworkSurgery + RT or RT alone; SBRT for radioresistant tumors
AVMSpetzler-Martin (size, eloquence, deep venous drainage)SRS (obliteration over 2–3 years)
Trigeminal neuralgiaClinical diagnosis; failed medicationsSRS to the nerve root (70–90 Gy max)
Glomus / paraganglioma, chordomaSkull base locationSRS/fractionated RT (glomus); surgery + high-dose RT, often protons (chordoma)
Benign CNS tumors are often treated on imaging alone: if it looks like a meningioma or an acoustic neuroma and it's growing, radiation is an option without a biopsy.
Quick check: a 1.2 cm intracanalicular-plus-CPA vestibular schwannoma touches but doesn't compress the brainstem. Koos grade?▾

Koos III. I = intracanalicular; II = into the CPA without brainstem contact; III = touches the brainstem; IV = compresses/displaces it.

Quick check: a patient with breast cancer has back pain; MRI shows epidural tumor compressing the cord with no CSF visible around it. Bilsky grade and first drug?▾

Bilsky 3 (high-grade compression). Give dexamethasone right away, then urgent surgical evaluation and/or RT.

NCCN Workup by Tumor

What the NCCN Central Nervous System Cancers Guidelines recommend, simplified for learning. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

ImagingMRI brain with/without contrast (pre-op and within 72 h post-op)
SurgeryMaximal safe resection when feasible; stereotactic biopsy otherwise
PathologyWHO 2021 integrated diagnosis: IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, ATRX, TP53, TERT, EGFR, +7/−10, CDKN2A/B, H3 K27M, BRAF
ImagingMRI brain (thin slices for SRS); body staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT)
TissueBiopsy/resection if no known primary, long interval, or uncertain diagnosis
AssessNumber and size, symptoms, KPS, systemic disease and CNS-active systemic options; neurosurgery input
ImagingMRI with contrast (CT for bone/hyperostosis); DOTATATE PET can help define extent
DiagnosisImaging alone is often enough for small asymptomatic tumors; resection gives WHO grade
UrgentDexamethasone for neurologic deficit; MRI of the entire spine
AssessNeurologic status, Bilsky grade, SINS stability, tumor radiosensitivity, systemic disease
ConsultSpine surgery and radiation oncology the same day
Before biopsyHold corticosteroids if possible
StagingMRI brain, ophthalmology slit-lamp exam, CSF cytology (± MRI spine), body CT or PET, HIV test, ± bone marrow

Grading Tables

Grade 2Diffuse, atypia, low mitotic activity
Grade 3+ significant mitotic activity (anaplasia)
Grade 4+ necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation, or molecular criteria (IDH-wt: TERT/EGFR/+7−10; IDH-mut astro: CDKN2A/B)
Grade 1Benign; <4 mitoses/10 HPF, no brain invasion
Grade 2Brain invasion, or 4–19 mitoses/10 HPF, or 3 of 5 atypical features; chordoid/clear cell
Grade 3≥20 mitoses/10 HPF, frank anaplasia, TERT promoter mutation, or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion
Simpson I–VI complete + dura + bone; II complete + dura coagulated; III complete, dura left; IV subtotal; V biopsy
Koos IIntracanalicular
Koos IIInto the CPA, no brainstem contact
Koos IIIFills the CPA, contacts the brainstem
Koos IVCompresses the brainstem (surgery favored)
Age<50 = 1; 50–60 = 0.5; >60 = 0
KPS90–100 = 1; 70–80 = 0.5; <70 = 0
Number of mets1 = 1; 2–3 = 0.5; >3 = 0
Extracranial metsNone = 1; present = 0

Original 2008 GPA. The diagnosis-specific GPA (lung, breast, melanoma, GI, renal) uses different factors by cancer type.

0Bone only
1a / 1b / 1cEpidural, no thecal sac deformity / deforms the sac / touches the cord without compression
2Cord compression, CSF still visible
3Cord compression, no CSF visible
Size<3 cm = 1; 3–6 cm = 2; >6 cm = 3
Eloquent brainNo = 0; yes = 1
Deep venous drainageNo = 0; yes = 1

Grade = sum (I–V). Low-grade AVMs are good SRS or surgical candidates.

High-Yield Summary
  • Brain tumors have no TNM, so ask what the tumor is, where it is and how big it is, and how functional the patient is (KPS).
  • Workup is MRI with contrast, steroids for symptoms (but not before a lymphoma biopsy), and maximal safe resection or biopsy for tissue and molecular markers.
  • In the WHO 2021 system, IDH-wildtype is glioblastoma, IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion is oligodendroglioma, and IDH-mutant without codeletion is astrocytoma.
  • MGMT promoter methylation predicts benefit from temozolomide.
  • For brain metastases, count and measure the lesions, stage the rest of the body, and estimate prognosis with the GPA.

Treatment Paradigms.title: CNS Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
CNS treatment covers a lot of different tumors, but the decisions follow a few simple rules. Three questions decide nearly everything:

1
Can it be safely removed?

Maximal safe resection is first for most gliomas, large or symptomatic mets, and many meningiomas. Deep or eloquent: biopsy only.

2
How aggressive is it?

Benign → observe, or SRS/fractionated RT if growing. Malignant → RT ± chemo after surgery.

3
Focal or everywhere?

Limited lesions → focal RT (SRS). Widespread (many mets, CSF spread) → whole brain or craniospinal.

The Framework

The CNS treatment ladder

Paradigm 1: Limited Brain Metastases

  • SRS alone for 1–4 mets (and, in selected patients, up to 10 small ones: JLGK0901 found 5–10 did as well as 2–4).
  • Don't add WBRT routinely: NCCTG N0574 showed more cognitive decline with no survival gain (just better intracranial control).
  • Surgery for a large (>3–4 cm) lesion, significant mass effect or hydrocephalus, or when tissue is needed. Then cavity SRS (Mahajan; N107C).
  • Single-fraction doses (RTOG 90-05): ≤2 cm 24 Gy, 2–3 cm 18 Gy, 3–4 cm 15 Gy. Larger lesions/cavities: 27 Gy/3 or 30 Gy/5.
  • Follow with MRI every 2–3 months: new lesions get more SRS.
  • Radionecrosis (~5–10%) is the main late risk, higher with larger lesions and immunotherapy.

Paradigm 2: Extensive Brain Metastases or Poor Prognosis

  • HA-WBRT 30 Gy/10 + memantine (NRG CC001: less memory and cognitive decline than WBRT + memantine). Memantine alone helped in RTOG 0614.
  • Very poor prognosis (low KPS, uncontrolled systemic disease): best supportive care (steroids) is reasonable. QUARTZ: WBRT added no survival or quality-of-life benefit in poor-prognosis NSCLC.
  • SCLC tends to have many mets: WBRT (or SRS in selected patients with close MRI follow-up).
  • Consider CNS-active systemic therapy first for asymptomatic mets from EGFR/ALK lung cancer, HER2+ breast cancer, or melanoma on immunotherapy.
  • Leptomeningeal disease: focal RT to symptomatic sites, or proton craniospinal in selected patients; poor prognosis.

Paradigm 3: Glioblastoma

6 cycles adjuvant TMZ ± TTFields
  • Stupp (EORTC/NCIC): RT + TMZ improved median survival (14.6 vs 12.1 months) and 5-year survival (~10% vs 2%). Benefit is largest with MGMT methylation.
  • TTFields (tumor treating fields, EF-14) with adjuvant TMZ improved survival further (median ~21 vs 16 months).
  • Target: GTV = enhancement + cavity (± FLAIR); CTV = +1.5–2 cm (two-phase: FLAIR to 46 Gy, then boost to 60 Gy is also common).
  • Older or frail: 40 Gy/15 + TMZ (Perry), 25 Gy/5 (Roa), or TMZ alone if MGMT-methylated and very frail.
  • Recurrence: re-resection, re-irradiation (e.g., 35 Gy/10) in selected patients, bevacizumab, lomustine, trials.
Try it: 58-year-old, GBM, IDH-wildtype, MGMT unmethylated, gross total resection, KPS 90. Plan?▾

60 Gy/30 + concurrent TMZ, then adjuvant TMZ ± TTFields. Unmethylated tumors benefit less from TMZ, but Stupp is still standard for fit patients (trials are an option).

Paradigm 5: Meningioma

  • Small, asymptomatic: observe with MRI.
  • Symptomatic or growing: surgery if accessible.
  • RT for tumors that can't be removed safely (e.g., cavernous sinus, skull base), residual/recurrent disease, or older patients:
    • SRS 12–14 Gy for small tumors a few mm away from the optic apparatus (5-year control ~90–95%).
    • Fractionated RT 50.4–54 Gy for larger tumors or those touching the chiasm/optic nerve.
  • Grade 2: RT after subtotal resection (~59.4–60 Gy); after gross total resection, observation vs RT is being studied (ROAM, NRG BN003).
  • Grade 3: RT after surgery regardless of resection (~60 Gy).

Paradigm 6: Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma)

Small / not growing
Observe

Serial MRI and audiograms. Many never grow.

Growing, small to medium
SRS

12–13 Gy marginal dose (or 25 Gy/5, 50.4 Gy fractionated). ~95% control. Hearing declines over years; facial nerve injury is rare.

Large (Koos IV)
Surgery

Brainstem compression or hydrocephalus. SRS for residual tumor.

  • Keep the cochlea mean dose ≤4 Gy to improve hearing preservation. Expect temporary swelling (pseudoprogression) at 6–18 months after SRS.

Paradigm 7: Pituitary Adenoma and Craniopharyngioma

  • Prolactinoma: cabergoline first (even for large tumors).
  • Other adenomas: transsphenoidal surgery; RT for residual/recurrent tumor or persistent hormone excess.
    • Fractionated: 45–50.4 Gy (nonfunctioning), 50.4–54 Gy (functioning).
    • SRS: 14–16 Gy (nonfunctioning), 20–25 Gy (functioning), keeping the chiasm ≤8–10 Gy (needs ~3–5 mm distance).
    • Hormone levels fall slowly after RT (years). Hypopituitarism is the main late effect: lifelong endocrine follow-up.
  • Craniopharyngioma: limited surgery (spare the hypothalamus) + RT 50.4–54 Gy. Watch for cyst growth during RT (repeat imaging). BRAF-mutant papillary type responds to BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

Paradigm 8: CSF Tumors, Lymphoma, Spine, and Functional SRS

Medulloblastoma

Resection → craniospinal RT (23.4 Gy standard risk / 36 Gy high risk) + posterior fossa or tumor-bed boost to ~54 Gy + chemo. Protons reduce dose to the heart, gut, and growing bones.

Primary CNS Lymphoma

High-dose methotrexate-based chemo first. RT (WBRT, reduced dose ~23.4 Gy after complete response; 30–45 Gy for residual) for consolidation or when chemo isn't possible. Big neurotoxicity risk in older patients.

Spinal Cord Compression

Dexamethasone immediately. Fit, single level, high-grade compression or instability: surgery + RT (Patchell). Otherwise RT: 8 Gy/1, 20 Gy/5, 30 Gy/10. SBRT (e.g., 24 Gy/2) for radioresistant tumors or oligometastases.

Functional SRS

AVM: 16–25 Gy; obliteration in ~70–80% over 2–3 years (bleeding risk persists until then). Trigeminal neuralgia: 70–90 Gy max to the nerve root; pain relief in weeks to months.

High-Yield Summary
  • Limited brain metastases get SRS alone, and a resected metastasis gets SRS to the cavity.
  • Many brain metastases get hippocampal-avoidant whole-brain RT with memantine to protect memory.
  • Glioblastoma gets maximal safe resection, then 60 Gy in 30 fractions with temozolomide followed by adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp), with shorter courses for older or frail patients.
  • Lower-grade gliomas can be observed after surgery or treated with RT plus chemo (PCV or temozolomide), which improves survival.
  • Benign tumors (meningioma, vestibular schwannoma, pituitary adenoma) are observed, resected, or treated with SRS or fractionated RT, and spinal cord compression gets steroids plus surgery and/or RT.
